799.title: Ephrem the Syrian
799.hook: the harp of the Spirit, who taught theology through hymns sung by women's choirs
799.howItsDone: Syriac Christians still sing hymns attributed to Ephrem in their services, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians keep a feast day in his honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Xi'an stele, and your line was the luminous teaching: monks telling the faith in borrowed words. Which holy word of yours turned out to be borrowed? Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

Which do you remember better: the last sermon you heard, or the chorus of a song you haven't heard in years? A tune gets in under the door. In the cities of Syria and Mesopotamia, in the early centuries of the church, there was a deacon who seems to have known that well. Rival teachers were spreading their ideas in catchy songs. He didn't ban the songs. He wrote his own, and taught choirs of women to sing them. Syriac churches still sing hymns under his name. Today's word is his name.
screen: `A TUNE GETS IN UNDER THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Ephrem lived in Nisibis and later in Edessa, and he wrote in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit. He wrote sermons in verse and commentaries too, but what he's remembered for is hymns, long, intricate songs with refrains, full of pictures. The poet Jacob of Serugh, writing after him, describes the choirs. Ephrem saw that the women of the church had no voice in its teaching, so he gathered them into choirs and taught them his hymns, and they stood in the church and sang the faith out loud for everyone to hear. So the theology arrived on women's voices, set to tunes people could carry home. And what kind of theology was it? Not definitions. Ephrem was wary of people who wanted to pin God down, to search out and measure what can't be measured. Instead he used symbols. A pearl, formed in the dark of the sea, becomes a picture of Christ. The world itself, he said in effect, is full of signs pointing to its maker, the way a scripture is. You don't trap the mystery in a sentence. You circle it with images and sing. Paul's letter to the Colossians, in the King James Bible, describes this kind of church: "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs." Teaching, by singing. Paul's line and Ephrem's choirs meet there. Tradition also says he cared for the sick and the hungry in a time of famine, and he's honored as a saint by Orthodox, Catholic and Syriac churches alike. In Ephrem's churches, the faith wasn't only read. It was sung.
screen: then, large: `PSALMS AND HYMNS AND SPIRITUAL SONGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write theology as a song. That sounds grand. It isn't. Pick a tune you already know well, a lullaby, a jingle, anything. Then pick one picture for something you believe or wonder about God, or about what's holy. Bread. Light under a door. A pearl in the dark. Hum the tune, and try fitting a few of your own words about that picture to it. It doesn't need to rhyme. It doesn't need to be good. If you'd rather not sing, just hum, and hold the picture while you do. The bell holds the time.
Ephrem. A deacon and poet of Syria who taught the faith through hymns and images, sung by women's choirs. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit.
Your line: the harp of the spirit. Today, when a song gets stuck in your head, notice what it's teaching you. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: Hagia Sophia (537)
800.hook: a dome that seemed to hang from heaven; a later story says Justinian claimed he'd outdone Solomon
800.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians remember Hagia Sophia as the great church of Constantinople, and some Orthodox churches are built around a central dome with an image of Christ looking down from its center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephrem, and your line was the harp of the spirit: theology you could sing. What song got stuck in your head, and what was it teaching? Day eight hundred.

A historian named Procopius walks into a new church in Constantinople and tries to describe the roof. He can't quite manage it. The great dome, he writes, doesn't seem to rest on stone at all. It seems to hang from heaven on a golden chain. And the light, he says, doesn't seem to come in from outside. It seems to be born inside the place. There's a later story, too, that the emperor Justinian walked in on the day it was dedicated and said he had outdone Solomon, who built the temple in Jerusalem. Whether he said it or not, the story stuck. Today's word is the name of that church.

Hagia Sophia is Greek for holy wisdom. The church wasn't named for a saint called Sophia. It was named for the wisdom of God, and Paul, in the King James words, calls Christ "the wisdom of God." The book of Proverbs, in the King James Bible, pictures wisdom as a builder: "Wisdom hath builded her house." Here was a house built in her name. Procopius, who wrote about the emperor's buildings, is our eyewitness. He describes a dome so wide and so light that it seemed to float, and a ring of windows around its base, so the sun pours in just below the curve. That's the trick behind the hanging dome. The light comes in under it, and the solid part seems to lift off. Now the Solomon story. The Bible's Solomon, dedicating his own temple, said something humbler. In the King James words: "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?" So the builder of the temple in Jerusalem says no house can hold God. Some readers hear that as the honest center of any great church. The dome isn't a container for God. It's a shape that points past itself, an attempt to make stone and light say something about heaven. Hagia Sophia has had a long life since. It has been a cathedral, then a mosque, then a museum, and today it is a mosque again, prayed in by Muslims and visited by people of every faith and none. Orthodox Christians still remember it as the great church of Constantinople. Tomorrow and the days after, we'll come back to this city and what happened inside its churches. Today, just look up.

Here's the practice: look at a photo of the dome. If you have your phone, search for the inside of Hagia Sophia's dome, looking straight up, and let it fill the screen. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes go first to the ring of windows, the light coming in. Then up into the curve. Then to the very top. Don't analyze it. Just let it be big. If you pray, you can let Solomon's question sit with you as you look: will God indeed dwell on the earth? If you don't pray, simply notice what happens in you when you look up for a long time. The bell holds the time.
Hagia Sophia. Holy wisdom: the great church of Constantinople, whose dome seemed to hang from heaven on a ring of light.
Your line: a dome of light. Today, stand under one high ceiling, a station, a library, a tree, and look straight up for a full breath. Day eight hundred.

801.title: The icon wars
801.hook: emperors smashed icons; John of Damascus argued that since God became visible, he can be painted
801.howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians pray with icons and images, often lighting a candle or kissing an icon; some Protestant churches keep images and crosses, and others keep their walls plain out of care for the commandment against graven images.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hagia Sophia, and your line was a dome of light. Did you find a high ceiling and look straight up? Today we stay in the same city, and the walls of its churches. Day eight hundred one.

Workmen climb a ladder outside a palace gate in Constantinople. Above the gate hangs an image of Christ. They've been sent to take it down. Tradition says a crowd of ordinary people gathered at the foot of the ladder, and some of them were women, and they shook it until the man on it fell. Whether every detail happened that way or not, the story shows what was at stake. For a long stretch, on and off, Christians in the eastern empire fought over pictures: whether a church could hold an image of Christ, of Mary, of the saints, or whether those images had to go. Today's word is the name for breaking them.
screen: `A CROWD AT THE FOOT OF IT.`

segments.voice: Iconoclasm means image-breaking, and an iconoclast is an image-breaker. Today we use the word for anyone who smashes a tradition. Here it meant it literally. Some emperors ordered icons removed, plastered over, or destroyed, and people who defended them were punished. It's easy to make the iconoclasts the villains. Be fair to them. Their argument came straight from scripture. The commandment, in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." They worried that Christians were bowing to wood and paint, and that God, who has no body, can't be pictured at all. That was a serious worry, held by believers. Then a monk named John, born in Damascus and living in a monastery near Jerusalem, outside the emperor's reach, wrote back. His answer turns on one idea. In the old days, he said in effect, God had no body and no face, so no one could make an image of him. But now God has been seen. The Word became flesh. He walked, ate, wept, was touched. So I paint what I have seen. I don't worship the wood, he said; I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake. Paul's letter to the Colossians gives him his key phrase. Christ, in the King James words, is "the image of the invisible God." If God has already made an image of himself, a human face, then a picture of that face isn't an insult to the invisible God. It's a way of saying he really came. Christians still differ here. Orthodox and Catholic Christians use icons and images in prayer. Some Protestant churches have pictures and crosses; some keep their walls deliberately plain, out of the same care for the commandment. Each side is trying to honor the same God.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT MAKE ANY GRAVEN IMAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an image of Christ. Any one: an icon, a painting, a stained-glass window, a small picture in a book, or one you find on your phone. Settle, and breathe. Look at the face. Notice who made it, roughly where, how they imagined him. Notice the eyes. If you pray, you can let the image be a window rather than the point, and pray through it. If you don't, simply look, and notice that someone, somewhere, painted this because they believed a face had been seen. The bell holds the time.
Iconoclasm. Image-breaking: the struggle in the eastern church over whether Christ and the saints could be pictured, and the name for smashing images.
Your line: the invisible became visible. Today, notice one face that shows you something you can't see directly: kindness, grief, patience. Day eight hundred one.

what a scholar hears: two scriptural arguments: no graven image, and the image of the invisible God made flesh.

802.title: The triumph of Orthodoxy (843)
802.hook: icons restored; Orthodox Christians still process with them on the first Sunday of Lent
802.howItsDone: On the Sunday of Orthodoxy, the first Sunday of Great Lent, Orthodox Christians carry icons in procession around or outside the church, and the restoration of the icons is proclaimed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, iconoclasm, the image-breaking, and your line was the invisible became visible. Whose face showed you something you couldn't see directly? Day eight hundred two.

On the first Sunday of Lent, in Orthodox churches, something unusual happens at the end of the service. People pick up icons, sometimes the ones from home, sometimes children carrying small ones, and walk with them in a procession around the church. Some parishes take them outside, around the building, into the street. It looks like a celebration, and it is. This Sunday has a name: the Sunday of Orthodoxy. It remembers the day, after the long fight over pictures, when the icons came back into the churches of Constantinople. Today's word is that homecoming.

The story goes like this. The image-breaking had come and gone and come again. A church council meeting at Nicaea had already defended icons, but later emperors banned them again. Then an emperor who opposed icons died, and his widow, the empress Theodora, ruled for their young son. Tradition says she had kept icons in private all along. She called the bishops together, the ban was lifted, and on the first Sunday of Lent there was a great procession into the church, carrying the images back in. That's the triumph of Orthodoxy. But what came back was not worship of wood and paint. The council at Nicaea had drawn a line. Icons, it said, are honored, kissed, given candles and incense. Worship belongs to God alone. And it borrowed a thought from Basil the Great: the honor given to an image passes on to the one it shows. Someone who kisses a photograph of a person they love isn't kissing the paper. That's the logic. Some Orthodox writers call icons windows: not the view itself, but a way of seeing through to it. That's where today's line comes from. Windows restored. Paul's second letter to the Corinthians says it this way in the King James Bible: God "hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." In the face. For the defenders of icons, the glory had a face. One more note. The word orthodoxy means right belief, and Christians use it in more than one sense. Here it names a particular feast of the Orthodox Church, which still keeps it, year after year, with the procession. Catholics and Protestants have their own ways with images, which we touched yesterday. Today belongs to this one Sunday, and its icons going home.
screen: `HONOR TO THE IMAGE, WORSHIP TO GOD.`
then, large: `IN THE FACE OF JESUS CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an image that helps you pray, or helps you remember what matters. It could be an icon or a cross. It could be a photo of someone you love, a picture of a place, a window you look out of. Pick it up or look at it. Settle, and breathe. Then do one small, physical thing to honor it: hold it carefully, wipe the dust off, set it somewhere it can be seen, light a candle near it if that's your way. If you pray, you can let it be a window, and pray through it. If you don't, let it be a reminder, and let the reminder do its work. The bell holds the time.
Orthodoxy, right belief. The feast marking the return of the icons to the churches, still kept by Orthodox Christians on the first Sunday of Lent with a procession of icons.
Your line: windows restored. Today, clean one actual window, or one screen, and look through it on purpose afterward. Day eight hundred two.

803.title: Boniface and the oak
803.hook: an English monk to the Germans, remembered for felling a sacred oak and dying a martyr
803.howItsDone: Boniface is honored as a saint and martyr, especially in Germany and the Netherlands; Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches remember him on his feast day, and his tomb is kept at Fulda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the triumph of Orthodoxy, and your line was windows restored: icons carried home. What did you look through on purpose? Day eight hundred three.

An axe bites into an enormous oak in a clearing in Hesse, in what is now Germany. The tree is sacred to the people who live here. The account calls it the oak of Jupiter, giving their god a Roman name. A crowd has gathered, and the crowd is cursing the man with the axe. He's a monk from England named Boniface, and the local Christians have urged him on. He makes one cut. Then, says the account, a great wind from above shakes the tree, and it comes crashing down. Today's word is that monk and that tree.

Our main source is a life of Boniface written by a priest named Willibald. Boniface was born in England, became a monk, and left a settled life to preach among the Germanic peoples across the sea. The oak is the scene his story turns on. In Willibald's telling, the people who had cursed him saw the tree fall and began to praise God instead. And Boniface used the timber to build a small chapel, dedicated to Saint Peter. The wood of the old shrine became the walls of the new one. Now the honest part. It was someone's holy tree. The people who gathered in that clearing weren't villains in their own story. And Christians have disagreed about how to meet another people's sacred places. Earlier on this path, Pope Gregory advised the missionaries in England to keep the old temples and take out only the idols: bless, don't destroy. Boniface's story goes the other way. Both are part of the church's story, and both are remembered. Then the ending. As an old man, Boniface went to preach in Frisia, near the North Sea. At dawn one morning his camp was attacked. Willibald says his companions reached for weapons, and Boniface stopped them. Scripture, he told them, teaches us not to repay evil for evil. In the King James words of Paul to the Romans: "Recompense to no man evil for evil." He was killed there with his companions. Tradition adds that he held up a book of the gospels over his head as the blow fell. So the man remembered for an axe died refusing a sword. Christians honor him as a martyr and as an apostle to the Germans.
screen: `A MONK FROM ENGLAND, ACROSS THE SEA.`
then, large: `RECOMPENSE TO NO MAN EVIL FOR EVIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing you need to stop worshiping. Not someone else's. Yours. Settle, and breathe. Christians reserve worship for God. But anything can quietly take that place: a phone, a number in a bank account, someone's approval, being right, being busy. Ask yourself, without hurry, what has grown too big. Don't fix it yet. Just name it, honestly, in a word. If you pray, you can hand that word to God and ask for help cutting it down to size. If you don't, simply hold the word, and notice how much room it takes up. The bell holds the time.
Boniface. The English monk who felled a sacred oak in Germany and built a chapel from its wood, and who died refusing to fight back.
Your line: cut it down. Today, take the word you named and cut its time by a little: ten minutes less, one check fewer. Day eight hundred three.

804.title: Cyril and Methodius
804.hook: two Greek brothers invent an alphabet so Slavs can worship in their own tongue
804.howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians keep a feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius, and some Slavic Orthodox churches still worship in Church Slavonic, the language of worship that grew from the brothers' translations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boniface, and your line was cut it down. Did you trim the thing you named, even a little? Day eight hundred four.

A prince in Moravia, in the heart of Central Europe, sends a message to the emperor in Constantinople. His people have heard Christian teachers, he says, but the teachers speak languages the people don't understand. Send us someone who can teach us in our own language. The emperor turns to two brothers from Thessalonica, a Greek city. In the old life of Methodius, he tells them that people from Thessalonica speak Slavonic well. Their names were Constantine and Methodius. Constantine is better known by the name he took as a monk at the end of his life: Cyril. There was one problem. The Slavs had no alphabet. Today's word is the two brothers who made one.

Our main sources are two old lives of the brothers, written in Slavonic by their followers. The life of Constantine says that he prayed, and then made the letters, and began to translate the gospel. And it gives the first words he wrote down, the opening of John: in the beginning was the Word. So the new letters began with the Word. Scholars call the alphabet he made Glagolitic. A later alphabet, built on Greek letters, came to carry Cyril's name: Cyrillic, still in use today. Not everyone was pleased. The life of Constantine says that in Venice he met clergy who insisted that God may be worshiped only in three languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin, the languages written on Christ's cross. Constantine answered them with scripture. Doesn't the rain fall on everyone? Doesn't the sun shine on all? And he quoted the Psalms, in the King James words: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." And he cited Paul, who said he would rather speak five words that people understand than ten thousand in a tongue they don't. Then there's Pentecost, in Acts, when the crowd asks, in the King James words: "how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" The brothers took that question as a commission. The road was hard. Methodius, after Cyril died, faced opposition and was even imprisoned. But the Slavonic worship they began lived on, and Church Slavonic is still prayed in some Orthodox churches today. Orthodox and Catholic Christians both honor the brothers, and they are sometimes called apostles to the Slavs.
screen: `A PRINCE ASKS FOR HIS OWN LANGUAGE.`
then, large: `EVERY MAN IN OUR OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn a word in another alphabet. Here's one in Cyrillic, the alphabet named for Cyril: slovo. It means word, the Word that was in the beginning. If you can, look it up. Its letters sound like S, L, O, V, O, though the first looks like a C and the fourth like a B. Settle, and breathe. Say it slowly: SLO-vo. Trace the shapes with your finger, in the air or on your palm. If you pray, you can let it carry you to the opening line of John. If you don't, just notice how strange and how ordinary it is to learn one word in someone else's script. The bell holds the time.
Glagolitic. The alphabet Cyril and Methodius made so the Slavs could hear scripture and worship in their own tongue.
Your line: in their own tongue. Today, say something kind to someone in the words they use, not yours: their slang, their language, their way. Day eight hundred four.

805.title: Vladimir's envoys (988)
805.hook: Kyiv's prince sends envoys to find a faith; at Hagia Sophia they didn't know if they were in heaven or on earth
805.tomorrow: Block close: the first thousand years
805.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians in Ukraine, Russia and Belarus remember the baptism of Kyiv and Saint Vladimir, and Orthodox worship gives great care to beauty: icons, chant, incense and light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyril and Methodius, who made the Glagolitic alphabet, and your line was in their own tongue: an alphabet so people could pray in their own language. Whose words did you borrow to be kind? Day eight hundred five.

Some travelers come home from a long trip and can't stop talking. Others come home and struggle to find words at all. A chronicle from Kyiv tells of a few men who came home the second way. Their prince, Vladimir, had sent them out to see how different peoples worshiped. They traveled, they watched, and at last they reached Constantinople, the city of the great church we stood under five days ago. When they returned, they tried to describe it, and what came out was not a report. It was a confession of being lost for words. Today's word is those travelers.

The story comes from the Primary Chronicle, a history written in Kyiv later, by monks looking back. The chronicle says Vladimir received visitors from several peoples, each describing their faith, and then sent his own envoys to see for themselves. We'll leave aside what the chronicle has them say about each place. What it remembers most is Constantinople. The Greeks, it says, led the envoys into the church where they worship their God. And the envoys reported, in paraphrase: we did not know whether we were in heaven or on earth. There is no such splendor or beauty anywhere on earth, and we cannot describe it. We only know that God dwells there among people. We cannot forget that beauty. That's the heart of it. Not an argument. An experience of worship. In the chronicle's telling, Vladimir was baptized, and then the people of Kyiv were called down to the river and baptized together in the Dnieper. Historians read the chronicle carefully; it was written later, and it shapes the story. Christians in Ukraine, Russia and Belarus look back to that baptism as a beginning. There's an older echo here. Jacob, in Genesis, wakes from a dream at Bethel and says, in the King James words: "How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Same astonishment: a place on earth that felt like heaven's doorway. Jacob set up a stone to mark it. The envoys carried home a sentence.
screen: `HEAVEN OR EARTH? WE DID NOT KNOW.`
then, large: `THIS IS THE GATE OF HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enter a beautiful place slowly. If you're somewhere with a doorway, a garden, a church, even a kitchen with good light, step into it as if you'd traveled a long way to get there. If you can't move right now, close your eyes and walk into a beautiful place you remember, one step at a time. Settle, and breathe. Notice the light first. Then the sound. Then the smell. Don't describe it to yourself. Let it be bigger than your words. If you pray, you can let Jacob's line sit with you: this is none other but the house of God.
